question: Sushi can contain vegetables or cooked seafood. Which part links these different versions?
note: Sushi rice is dressed with vinegar, often with sugar and salt. Raw fish is one possible accompaniment, rather than the ingredient that every version must contain.

question: A bowl of Japanese soba arrives chilled beside a dipping sauce. What should the diner make of that?
choices: It is a normal way to serve the noodles
The sauce should be heated at the table
The noodles need a final dip in boiling water
The dish is meant as a sweet final course
note: Soba can be served cold with a dipping sauce or hot in broth. The buckwheat noodles belong to more than one kind of meal.

question: Tempura feels thoroughly Japanese, but its development was influenced by visitors from which European country?
note: Portuguese visitors helped introduce the style of frying that developed into tempura several centuries ago. By the Edo period, it was being sold from street stalls as a quick meal. Even the little scraps of fried batter have a use, becoming crunchy additions to noodle dishes.

question: The name oyakodon means “parent-and-child bowl.” Which ingredients explain it?
note: The parent is the chicken and the child is the egg, cooked together and served over rice. The same naming joke can apply to a seafood bowl with salmon and salmon roe. A bowl pairing egg with an unrelated meat, such as beef, may be called tanindon, a “stranger bowl.”

question: Okonomiyaki contains words meaning “as you like”. What does that suggest about this Japanese griddle dish?
choices: Its price is chosen by the diner
Its name changes with the season
Its cooking time is chosen after serving
note: The savoury pancake can combine cabbage and other ingredients in different ways. In some restaurants the table has its own griddle, so diners help make the meal.

question: A Japanese sweet may use a filling that many visitors associate with savoury cooking. What commonly fills dorayaki pancakes?
note: Azuki beans are cooked into a sweet paste and sandwiched between two small pancakes. Beans can play a dessert role as comfortably as a savoury one.

question: Japanese curry has Indian roots, but through which country did it reach Japan in the nineteenth century?
note: Curry came to Japan through Britain, where an adapted version of the Indian dish had already become popular. Japanese curry developed into a thick sauce, commonly served with rice and made at home with blocks of curry roux. It also found its way inside bread, giving Japan the filled snack called kare-pan.

question: Miso soup and tofu look very different. Which crop is used to make both?
note: Fermentation turns soybeans into miso, while a different process produces tofu. A single bowl of soup can bring together two forms of the same crop.

question: What makes drinking matcha different from steeping ordinary tea leaves and removing them?
choices: The powdered leaves are mixed into the drink
The leaves are steeped and strained several times
The tea is fermented after it is brewed
The leaf stems replace the leaf blades
note: Matcha is finely powdered green tea whisked into water. A bamboo whisk helps blend the powder instead of removing it as spent leaves.

question: A Japanese railway traveller buys an ekiben, a boxed meal. What can it offer beyond food for the journey?
choices: A taste of the region where it is sold
A menu fixed by the railway nationwide
A meal made only from preserved foods
A dish selected to match the train’s name
note: Ekiben often show off regional food. Vendors once sold them through carriage windows, making the station part of the meal’s identity.

question: Tokyo’s earlier name survives in the term for a major period of Japanese history. What was it?
note: Edo became the seat of Tokugawa rule in 1603, long before it received the name Tokyo. In 1868, the Meiji Restoration ended the shogunate and the city took its new name. The old name survives in “Edo period,” used for the centuries of Tokugawa government.

question: A visitor looking for Gion’s traditional streets and wooden townhouses would go to which former imperial capital?
note: Gion is one of Kyoto’s best-known historic districts, associated with geiko and their apprentices, maiko. Kyoto also preserves machiya, the narrow wooden townhouses that shaped its streets. These buildings help give the former imperial capital a very different feel from the high-rise districts of modern Tokyo.

question: Why do deer have such a special place around Nara’s Kasuga Taisha shrine?
choices: They are regarded as divine messengers
They were trained to guard the palace
They were imported as royal hunting animals
They were bred to pull temple carts
note: The deer’s religious association helps explain their protected place in the city. Visitors now know them for roaming the park and approaching people with deer crackers.

question: Why is Himeji nicknamed the White Heron Castle?
choices: Its pale walls and roofs suggest a bird
Its moat was used to breed white herons
Its founder was named after that bird
Its towers were designed as nesting boxes
note: The white surfaces and spreading rooflines suggest wings. Behind that graceful appearance are gates, walls and winding defensive approaches.

question: Mount Fuji’s World Heritage listing recognises more than a dramatic landscape. What is central to it?
choices: Its role in pilgrimage and art
Its unique collection of alpine wildlife
Its history as a centre of mineral extraction
Its importance to modern winter sports
note: The inscription includes shrines, routes and other places associated with devotion to the mountain. Fuji is a cultural landscape as well as a volcano.

question: Japan opened its first Shinkansen line just before hosting which 1964 event?
choices: The first Japanese Formula One Grand Prix
note: The Tokyo–Shin-Osaka service began on 1 October 1964. The new railway and the Olympics brought two lasting images of modern Japan into view together.

question: Sapporo’s huge snow festival began with sculptures made by whom?
note: Students made six snow sculptures in Odori Park in 1950. A modest local event grew into the festival associated with the city today.

question: Karate is recognised worldwide as Japanese. Which island region shaped it through local traditions and Chinese influences?
note: Okinawa was once the centre of the Ryukyu Kingdom, with its own overseas connections. Karate’s roots reflect that distinct history within present-day Japan.

question: On the back of Fushimi Inari’s famous red gates, what do many inscriptions record?
choices: Who donated the gate and when
Which emperor passed through it last
The weight of timber used to build it
note: Individuals and businesses donate torii gates to the shrine. The famous paths are also a visible record of those contributions.

question: What holds the great torii of Itsukushima Shrine upright where it stands in the sea?
choices: Bolts fixing it to a stone base
Steel cables tied to the shore
note: Nothing sinks the gate into the seabed or ties it down. It weighs about sixty tonnes, seven of them stones packed into the box of its top beam, and stands under that weight alone; the two main pillars were cut from camphor trees more than five hundred years old. The present gate dates from 1875, and at low tide people can walk out to it.

question: Japan’s cherry-blossom gatherings are called hanami. What are people gathering to do?
note: Hanami means flower viewing and is especially associated with cherry blossoms. People gather beneath the trees to enjoy their short season, often with a picnic. Because the blossoms open at different times across Japan, the season moves through the country rather than arriving everywhere on a single day.

question: Tanabata’s lovers are represented by Vega and Altair. What separates them in the traditional story?
note: The lovers are allowed to meet once a year. Wishes written on coloured paper and hung from bamboo bring the celestial story into everyday celebrations.

question: Why are carp-shaped streamers flown for Children’s Day?
choices: They express hopes for strength and perseverance
They ask for a plentiful fishing season
They commemorate the start of spring planting
note: A legend tells of a carp overcoming a waterfall and becoming a dragon. The streamers turn that image of effort into a wish for children.

question: At Setsubun, people throw beans while calling for demons to leave. What are they welcoming in?
note: The ritual marks the seasonal turn before spring in the traditional calendar. A family member may wear a demon mask, making the symbolic eviction a household event.

question: At the lowered entrance area of a Japanese home, what does a visitor normally do before stepping inside?
choices: Leave all bags in the street
note: The genkan separates outdoor footwear from indoor floors. The custom is especially practical where people sit or sleep close to the floor.

question: The size of a traditional Japanese room is often described by counting what?
note: Tatami mats serve as both flooring and a familiar way of describing room size, though their dimensions vary by region. A traditional room can change purpose through the day. Bedding is laid out at night and put away afterwards, leaving the same floor available for sitting or other activities.

question: Why is a yukata a familiar sight at Japanese summer festivals?
choices: It is a lighter, informal garment
It is a uniform worn by festival workers
It is formal dress reserved for religious rites
It identifies the wearer’s home prefecture
note: The yukata is a casual relative of formal kimono dress. It is held with an obi and suits summer occasions such as fireworks festivals.

question: The snow monkeys photographed soaking in Japanese hot springs are which animals?
note: At Jigokudani, macaques have a hot-spring pool of their own. Young monkeys had earlier begun entering a bath at a nearby inn; the familiar image has a local history.

question: A common custom is to paint one eye on a daruma doll when setting a goal. When is the other painted?
note: A daruma can act as a visible reminder of an unfinished ambition, with the second eye waiting until the goal is met. The doll represents Bodhidharma, associated with the founding of Zen Buddhism. Its weighted base lets it spring upright after being tipped, reinforcing its association with perseverance.

question: What is the raised paw of a maneki-neko meant to be doing?
note: The familiar shop cat is making a beckoning gesture intended to welcome good fortune or customers. With the paw facing outward, the gesture can look like a wave to visitors used to beckoning with the palm upward. Several stories explain the cat’s origin, so no single legend should be treated as settled history.

question: Who wrote The Tale of Genji, about a thousand years ago?
note: She served the empress Shōshi and is known as Murasaki Shikibu, but that is a nickname: Murasaki is the heroine of her own book, and Shikibu comes from her father’s post at court. Her real name is not known. She also kept a diary at court, in which she is sharp about the other famous woman writer of the day, Sei Shōnagon.

question: Hokusai’s Great Wave belongs to a series of views of which landmark, shown small in the distance?
note: The wave dominates the image, but Fuji is part of its composition. The print belongs to Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji and uses the imported pigment Prussian blue.

question: Noh theatre often uses a fixed mask. What helps the performer give a character expression?
choices: Controlled movement and the angle of the mask
Interchangeable mouth pieces fitted between lines
A second performer speaking through the mask
A painted screen that changes behind the face
note: Small changes in a mask’s angle can change how its expression is perceived. Noh brings mask, movement, voice and music together.

question: In Bunraku theatre, where are the puppeteers during the performance?
choices: Behind a screen showing only shadows
note: Three performers operate a main puppet, sharing its head, hands and feet. The audience can see the human work that creates the character.

question: Kabuki is associated with male performers, including men in female roles. Who helped begin the form?
note: Izumo no Okuni performed in Kyoto in the early seventeenth century. Women were later banned from the public stage, changing who could perform the tradition.

question: Which bird is especially associated with origami and the custom of folding a thousand for a wish?
note: Folding a thousand cranes, senbazuru, goes with a wish for recovery or long life. Sadako Sasaki, who was two when the bomb fell on Hiroshima, folded cranes in hospital before she died of leukaemia in 1955. A popular version says she died short of a thousand, but her brother and the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum say she passed it, and cranes are still left for her at the Children’s Peace Monument.

question: In ikebana, what matters besides the flowers themselves?
choices: The stems, container and surrounding space
Matching every stem to exactly the same height
Packing the container so no gaps remain
Arranging flowers strictly by their market value
note: The arrangement considers lines and spaces as well as blossoms. Its setting may be a tokonoma alcove, sometimes alongside a hanging scroll.

question: What makes a kintsugi repair distinctive?
choices: The joins are made visible with precious metal
The broken piece is ground into fresh clay
The entire pot is covered in opaque paint
The cracks are concealed beneath a fabric sleeve
note: Lacquer holds the fragments together and gold highlights the seams. Related repair techniques use silver or lacquer alone; in each case, repair can become part of the object’s appearance.

question: The shamisen reached Japan through the Ryukyu Islands. What kind of instrument is it?
note: It has three strings and is usually played with a large plectrum. Its sound became part of Kabuki and puppet theatre after the instrument’s arrival through the islands.

question: In the Japanese New Year custom kakizome, what might someone put on paper?
choices: Words expressing a hope for the year
Names of all the guests expected at home
An inventory of gifts received in December
A list of the year’s national holidays
note: Kakizome is the first calligraphy of the year. Brush and ink turn a wish or resolution into something made by hand.

question: Which Studio Ghibli film won the animated feature Oscar at the 2003 Academy Awards?
note: Hayao Miyazaki wrote and directed it, and it opened in Japan in July 2001. A year before the Oscar it shared the Golden Bear at the Berlin festival with Bloody Sunday, the first time an animated film had won Berlin’s top prize. The films it beat for the Oscar included Ice Age and Lilo & Stitch.

question: The original Godzilla reached cinemas in 1954. Which anxiety helped shape its destructive monster?
choices: The possibility of invasion from space
note: The black-and-white film was made after nuclear war and amid hydrogen-bomb testing in the Pacific. Its monster story carried fears that were very close to contemporary life.

question: What did Nintendo originally make when it was founded in 1889?
note: Fusajiro Yamauchi began Nintendo in Kyoto by making hanafuda playing cards. The company’s history in games therefore began long before electronics. In 1959 it marketed cards featuring Walt Disney characters, decades before Mario became its best-known face.

question: Why might a player in Japan remember Red and Green as the first Pokémon games, while an American remembers Red and Blue?
choices: The first releases differed between markets
The names changed between cartridge printings
Players chose a colour after finishing the story
The television series used different titles
note: Red and Green appeared in Japan in 1996. North America received Red and Blue in 1998, so two memories of the beginning can both be right.

question: According to Sanrio’s character profile, Hello Kitty was born in the suburbs of which city?
note: Hello Kitty’s official profile places her birth in suburban London and gives her the name Kitty White. It measures her height as five apples and her weight as three apples. Her family also includes a twin sister, Mimmy, giving the character a small fictional biography beyond the familiar face.

question: Doraemon is a robot cat, yet he has no ears. What happened to them in his backstory?
choices: A robot mouse chewed them off
He traded them for his pocket of gadgets
They folded into antennae inside his head
He removed them to travel through time
note: The story gives a reason for both his round silhouette and his fear of mice. A cat frightened of a mouse becomes part of the character’s joke.

question: In sumo, which part of a wrestler’s body may touch the ground without losing the bout?
note: A wrestler loses by touching the ground with anything other than the soles of the feet, or by stepping outside the ring. The contest takes place in a dohyo about 4.5 metres across. Sumo’s ceremonies preserve traces of its earlier role in rituals giving thanks for the harvest.

question: Modern judo began with Jigoro Kano’s small school. Where did its first students practise?
note: Kano began in 1882 with nine students. He linked physical training to education long before judo became an Olympic sport.

question: Why are bamboo swords and protective armour central to kendo practice?
choices: They allow contact while reducing injury risk
They make every strike easier for judges to hear
They recreate the weight of battlefield equipment
They limit movement to the upper body
note: Kendo developed from swordsmanship. Its practice equipment lets participants train through contact without using sharpened steel blades.

question: The word karaoke combines Japanese words meaning what?
note: Kara means “empty,” and oke is a shortening of okesutora, the Japanese borrowing of “orchestra.” The name describes an accompaniment that leaves room for the participant’s voice.
